task: Write one sentence of your own using the word adept. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know adept should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Long winters made Aunt Vera adept at mending nets, her shuttle moving faster than the eye could follow.
Capable is milder than adept — the job gets done correctly, and that is all capable promises; adept does the same job with a polish that years of repetition buy.
Masterly goes further than adept — the adept sailor wins the regatta; a masterly one seems to teach the wind itself how the race should go.

Proficient means solidly capable: you meet the standard reliably, and nobody worries about the result. Adept sits a rung higher — the skill repeated until the difficult parts stop showing. Every adept sailor is proficient; plenty of proficient sailors still sweat the tricky moorings.

Practiced tells you where the skill came from — repetition, hours logged — without saying how far it climbed; a practiced apology can still be a clumsy one. Adept names the height itself: skill so complete the work looks easy. You can be practiced and mediocre, never adept and mediocre.

The camp counselor's aptitude for knots showed on the very first hitch.
Adept means extremely skilled.

The station's traffic reporter is adept at reading the city: give her three camera feeds and a rainfall report, and she will tell you which bridge will jam eight minutes before it does, rerouting half the morning's drivers around a stall they never see.
Adept is the right word because adept means extremely skilled — not merely able to do the job, but so practiced that the hard parts look routine.
Skilled says you clear the bar; adept says you clear it every time, without visible effort, usually after years of repetition.
Adept is broad praise for practiced, high-level skill at an activity — adept at chess, at coding, at calming toddlers.
When the skill lives in the hands specifically, this unit's deft is sharper; when it is cleverness in a tight spot, adroit; for the loud, demonstrated feats themselves, prowess.

Customers at the co-op shop learned to bring Rosa the bikes nobody else would touch.
A seized crank, a wheel bent in a crash, a vintage shifter with no parts made since 1974 — she worked without hurry, and the hard jobs somehow finished early.
New mechanics watched her true a wheel and swore the rim straightened itself.
Rosa waved the praise off.
Everyone in the shop, she said, could fix a flat correctly, and most could handle the standard repairs reliably.
What set her apart was what thirty years had done: made her adept, so extremely skilled that the difficulty disappeared from the outside.
The apprentices logged their hours and hoped.
Hours alone, the manager warned them, buy repetition; they do not always buy that.
